The removal of the citizenship question from the census was based on 
concerns that that question would dissuade substantial numbers of residents 
from responding to the Census Bureau’s questionnaires. And the plaintiffs’ 
lawsuit in Department of Commerce v. New York was predicated upon the belief 
that adding a citizenship question would produce a significant undercount, 
particularly in urban areas with substantial numbers of undocumented 
residents. Because the census data is used to determine the number of 
representatives allocated to each state, the amount of funds that states or 
locahties receive under various federal formula grants, and for other purposes 
affecting local interests, plaintifis claimed that they would be harmed by the 
imdercount that would predictably result from adding the citizenship question. 
The plaintifis raised a number of legal claims, but for present purposes the 
important ones were the claims that the Commerce Department’s decision was 
arbitrary and capricious under the Administrative Procedure Act and 
predicated on a rationale that was a mere pretext for the Secretary’s real 
purposes in reinstating the citizenship question in the census.
In the course of the proceedings before the district court, the district judge 
became convinced that the record that had initially been suppfied by the 
Department of Commerce was incomplete. The judge, therefore, ordered that 
the record be expanded to include a large trove of communications concerning 
the decision to add the citizenship question, both within the Department of 
Commerce and in communication with other agencies. The court also 
authorized extra-record discovery to further amplify the record and to seek to 
estabhsh the Secretary’s real reasons for authorizing the addition of the 
citizenship question. On the basis of the amplified record the district court 
found both that the decision was arbitrary under the Administrative Procedure 
Act and that the reasons given by the Secretary for including the question were 
pretextual. In the district court’s view the risks of a substantial undercount if 
the citizenship question were included on the 2020 census, and the availability 
of alternative methods for providing data on citizenship, rendered the 
Secretary’s decision to include the question unreasonable. The court also found 
that the sole reason provided by the Secretary for including the question, a 
request by the Justice Department that the question be included as an aid in 
enforcing the Voting Rights Act, was fabricated. The record revealed that the 
Secretary had come into office determined to include a citizenship question in 
the census questionnaire and had sohcited the Justice Department request, a 
request that seems to have been only reluctantly provided.
Because of the urgency of providing a definitive resolution in time for the 
printing of the 2020 census questionnaires the Supreme Court accepted 
expedited review of the district court decision without going through review by 
a court of appeals. Chief Justice Roberts delivered the opinion of the Court
